title: Chapter 23: Secure and Robust Java Development
description: Integrate security into ordinary design and review. Learners threat-model assets and entry points, prevent injection with structured APIs, constrain paths and parsers, handle secrets and passwords with approved facilities, enforce CPU, memory, time, queue, and output limits, and maintain dependency, configuration, patch, and audit evidence suitable for production ownership.

lessons.title: Threat modeling, assets, actors, authentication, and authorization
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Threat modeling, assets, actors, authentication, and authorization

## Start with assets and authority
List valuable data, actors, entry points, and trust boundaries. A task service may protect private tasks and administrative operations. Authentication identifies an actor; authorization decides whether that actor may access this particular task.

```java
if (!task.ownerId().equals(currentUser.id())) {
    throw new AccessDeniedException();
}
```
This is a conceptual fragment with application-defined types. Perform ownership checks on the server for every relevant operation. A hidden UI button or a validated task ID does not grant permission.

## Threat reasoning
Ask how an attacker could read another user's data, alter ownership, exhaust capacity, or exploit a dependency. Apply least privilege to database users and filesystem access. Deny access when essential identity or policy information is missing.

## Practice
Threat-model create/read/update/delete and list endpoints. Include enumeration of another user's IDs and mass assignment of owner fields. Write tests for authenticated-but-unauthorized actors. Record each mitigation next to its threat and residual assumptions, rather than producing an unconnected list of security features.

lessons.title: Secrets, cryptography, password storage, TLS, and sensitive data
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Secrets, cryptography, password storage, TLS, and sensitive data

## Secrets have lifecycles
Credentials need controlled provisioning, restricted access, rotation, revocation, and redaction. Environment variables are a delivery mechanism, not a guarantee that a secret cannot appear in diagnostics. Never commit credentials or include them in URLs, exception messages, logs, or generated artifacts.

## Use established cryptography
Use reviewed high-level APIs and authenticated encryption with correct nonce/key management. Passwords need a dedicated slow, salted password-hashing algorithm through a maintained library; plain SHA-256 is not password storage. TLS authenticates and encrypts transport when certificate verification is preserved; “trust all certificates” removes essential protection.

```java
var random = new java.security.SecureRandom();
byte[] tokenBytes = new byte[32];
random.nextBytes(tokenBytes);
```
This creates unpredictable bytes, not a complete authentication system. Tokens still need safe encoding, storage, expiry, scope, and revocation.

## Practice
Audit a sample repository for hard-coded secrets and sensitive logging. Design token rotation and a lost-token response. Explain what encryption at rest does not protect against if the application itself is compromised. Avoid implementing your own cipher or password-hashing scheme.

exercises.title: Secrets, cryptography, password storage, TLS, and sensitive data: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why is plain SHA-256 unsuitable for password storage?
choices: It is a fast general hash rather than a dedicated slow password hash
It is fine as long as a random salt is added
hints: Think about how many hashes per second a fast general-purpose digest lets an attacker try against stolen hashes, salted or not, compared to a deliberately slow password-hashing algorithm.

lessons.title: Dependency scanning, secure configuration, patching, and audit evidence
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Dependency scanning, secure configuration, patching, and audit evidence

## Secure configuration is part of delivery
Track runtime, framework, and transitive dependency versions. Review advisories and upgrade with compatibility tests. An SBOM records components but is not evidence that they are safe. Remove unused dependencies and exposed endpoints to reduce attack surface.

```text
Release review:
- controlled dependency versions and provenance
- no embedded credentials
- restricted administrative endpoints
- verified TLS and authorization defaults
- tested rollback and migration compatibility
```
This release checklist belongs in the engineering workflow, not a claim that every item can be proven by a scanner.

## Fail closed where required
If signing keys or authorization configuration are missing, starting in a permissive mode can expose data. Validate essential settings at startup. Distinguish development conveniences from production defaults explicitly.

## Practice
Review a deployment that exposes a debug endpoint, prints configuration including secrets, and uses a privileged database account. Propose targeted corrections and tests. Document how a critical dependency update is assessed, deployed, and verified. Preserve audit events with safe identifiers and a retention/access policy.

exercises.title: Dependency scanning, secure configuration, patching, and audit evidence: concept check
hints: Distinguish knowing exactly what components and versions ship in the build from having verified that none of them carry a known or future flaw.

lessons.title: Chapter 23 assessment and deliberate practice
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 23 assessment

Bring together threat modeling, injection-safe APIs, secret and password handling, resource limits, and dependency/audit hygiene to solve the decision scenario and repair **Redact the entire short secret**, where a short secret is printed in full instead of being masked. Write a prediction before running the debugger and preserve the intended redaction behavior when fixing it.

The function exercise is a bounded practice task, not proof of every chapter competency. Complete the implementation and external practice described in the five lessons as well. Review the changed source for its contract, then explain the relevant tradeoff without consulting the answer.

exercises.title: Chapter 23 implementation lab: redact
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `redact`. For secrets longer than four characters return *** plus the final four; otherwise return ***. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Input is non-null. This masking rule is a practice contract; real logs should usually omit credentials entirely.
hints: Decide the length boundary first: secrets of four characters or fewer must be fully masked, and only longer secrets reveal a trailing slice.
Check both an empty string and a secret exactly at the four-character boundary before trusting the substring math for longer inputs.

exercises.title: Redact the entire short secret
exercises.instructionMarkdown: The supplied condition treats a secret up to and including four characters as safe to print unmasked, but a short secret must be fully redacted like any other. Repair the comparison so the program writes exactly `***`. Preserve the demonstrated redaction logic and explain why your fix changes the result; do not replace it with a hard-coded print. Output tests verify the result; preserving the intended redaction behavior requires source review.
hints: Short secrets must never be logged in full.
